top.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
top.description: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on Large Language Models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied up energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 in the United States. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference that could be tracked moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. That reduced the list to 403 data centers with an average electrical capacity of about 40 megawatts. Read full article Comments

top.title: Senate Agriculture Committee to Hear Trump’s CFTC Nominees Tuesday
top.description: Bitcoin Magazine Senate Agriculture Committee to Hear Trump’s CFTC Nominees Tuesday The Senate Agriculture Committee will hear President Donald Trump’s two nominees to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) on Tuesday, a confirmation hearing that comes as the derivatives regulator has only one sitting commissioner. The committee scheduled the session for 3 p.m. Eastern in Room 106 of the Dirksen Senate Office Building. The White House sent the nominations to the Senate on Nov. 12. The nominees are Nathan Anonick of Virginia and Matthew Rowland of the District of Columbia. The hearing notice says to check back for live video, and the committee has not posted written testimony. Trump nominated the pair last week as part of a bipartisan slate for the CFTC and the Securities and Exchange Commission, a step that would begin to refill two regulators that have been operating short-handed. Who the nominees are Anonick serves on the Republican staff of the Senate Agriculture Committee under Chairman John Boozman of Arkansas. He was nominated to the seat once held by former Chairman Rostin Behnam, for a term ending June 19, 2031. A 2023 committee release said Anonick joined the panel in 2022 to manage a portfolio that includes cryptocurrencies, futures markets and derivatives, and that he had previously worked at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation as a resolution policy specialist. Rowland is a CFTC attorney detailed to the committee’s Democratic staff under Ranking Member Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota. He would fill the remainder of former Commissioner Summer K. Mersinger’s term, which expires April 13, 2028. Both nominees come from the committee that oversees the CFTC. CFTC Chairman Michael Selig called them “two strong bipartisan picks” and said he looks forward to working with them “upon their confirmation by the US Senate.” Kristin N. Johnson and Steven Levine, the two SEC nominees from the same White House list, are on the agenda for a Senate Banking Committee nominations hearing at 10 a.m. Thursday in Dirksen 538. A CFTC commission of one The CFTC can seat up to five commissioners, with no more than three from the same party. Chairman Michael S. Selig, sworn in Dec. 22, 2025, is currently the only sitting commissioner listed on the agency’s website. Even if the Senate confirms both nominees, two of the five seats would remain vacant. Each nominee still needs a committee vote and then confirmation by the full Senate. The Agriculture Committee has not scheduled that vote. The new Congress is seated in January. If the Senate does not confirm the nominations before then, they would typically be returned to the president and have to be sent again. top.title: Jackson scores as Senegal move closer to 2027 AFCON
top.description: Premier League duo Nicolas Jackson and El Hadji Malick Diouf scored on Monday as Senegal beat Sudan 4-2 to virtually clinch a place at the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations tournament. Cameroon trounced Namibia 3-0 and Benin snatched a late 1-0 win over the Central African Republic to move close to qualification for the marquee African competition. Senegal, Cameroon and Benin have 10 points each from four matches and could all be confirmed as qualifiers on Tuesday depending on the other result in their groups. Cameroon and Senegal are former AFCON champions while the furthest Benin have progressed is the round of 16 at the 2025 tournament. Jackson came to Africa last week, having scored nine goals in all competitions for Aston Villa this season. He opened the scoring in a 4-1 home win over Sudan last Thursday. He also broke the deadlock with a fourth-minute goal away to Sudan, who hosted the match in South Sudan because of a civil war in their homeland. Defender Diouf, who moved from relegated West Ham United to Brentford during the close season, doubled the lead midway through the first half. Sudan staged a second-half comeback to draw level after 75 minutes through goals from substitute Al Gozoli Nooh and Salaheldin Adil. But a late Senegalese rally saw Pathe Mboup restore the lead, then set up Paul Mendy to score in added time. – Cameroon romp – Senegal won the final of previous edition of the AFCON 1-0 in extra time over hosts Morocco last February. But CAF declared Morocco champions because most of the Senegalese team temporarily left the field to protest a penalty, which Morocco missed when play resumed. Senegal have asked the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) in Switzerland to overturn the CAF ruling and a decision is expected this month. It took Cameroon 12 minutes to score away to Namibia through Mahamadou Nagida. Goals from Ryan Fosso and Saidou Alioum in the second half completed the victory. Benin left it late to secure maximum points with debutant Ede Oloko netting in added time. The goal condemned the Central African Republic to a fourth straight loss. Elsewhere, Zimbabwe outplayed Equatorial Guinea 3-0 in Harare, Guinea beat Eritrea 3-1 in Cairo and a Jordan Ayew penalty earned Ghana an unimpressive 1-0 win over Somalia in Essipong. In the six matches on Monday, Zimbabwe were the only host nation to actually play at home. Central African Republic, Eritrea and Namibia do not have international-standard stadiums. A civil war that erupted in April 2023 prevents Sudan from playing in Khartoum and Somalia cannot stage AFCON qualifiers due to security concerns in the Horn of Africa. nigeria.title: Budget 2027: FG moves to slash overhead costs, directs MDAs to share facilities
nigeria.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief As the Federal Government prepares its 2027 budget, it is stepping up efforts to cut overhead expenditure by directing Ministries, Departments and Agencies (MDAs) to maximise the use of existing government-owned facilities instead of spending public funds on hotels and other privately owned venues for official meetings. The move is part of a broader cost-saving initiative by the Federal Ministry of Finance, through its Efficiency Office (E-Office), to eliminate avoidable expenditure, improve the utilisation of public assets and ensure value for money in government operations. According to Efe Ovuakporie, Head, Information and Public Relations Unit of the Federal Ministry of Finance, in a statement in Abuja on Monday evening, under the initiative, “The Office is working towards establishing a coordinated system that will enable MDAs to identify and access available meeting and conference facilities across government institutions, thereby reducing the need to hire commercial venues for official engagements.” She added, “A major component of the programme is the compilation of a comprehensive directory of meeting facilities owned by MDAs nationwide. The directory, which will be published on the Federal Ministry of Finance’s website upon completion, is expected to provide government institutions with information on available facilities and make it easier to locate suitable venues. “The arrangement will also enable MDAs with under-utilised conference facilities to generate revenue by making them available to other government institutions, while reducing pressure on government overhead budgets.” Ovuakporie said the initiative aligns with the Efficiency Office’s mandate to promote value for money, reduce overhead expenditure, monitor the utilisation of public assets and identify areas of waste across government institutions. In a related development, the Office recently inspected shared government facilities across the five South-Eastern states of Abia, Anambra, Ebonyi, Enugu and Imo, as part of efforts to identify underutilised public infrastructure and opportunities for cost savings. The inspection covered selected Federal Secretariats, Federal Polytechnics, Federal Medical Centres and Federal Universities. The exercise assessed the condition, availability, utilisation and maintenance of the facilities, with particular attention to areas where improved management could enhance productivity and reduce unnecessary government spending. Among the findings were under-utilised office spaces and facilities, deteriorating furniture, fittings and equipment, as well as inadequate maintenance of some offices and common areas. The inspection teams also identified opportunities to improve the utilisation of conference facilities and strengthen the organisation, storage and preservation of official records. nigeria.title: Gunmen kill Operation Rainbow commander, one other in Plateau
nigeria.description: By Golok Nanmwa Suspected gunmen have killed a newly graduated unit commander of the Plateau State-owned civilian security outfit, Operation Rainbow, and another person in an ambush in Bokkos Local Government Area of Plateau State. The victims were reportedly killed at about 3pm on Monday while returning from a condolence visit to Hurti village to their community in Tadai, Manguna District of Bokkos Local Government Area. The community leader, Machief Paul, who confirmed the incident to newsmen, said both victims were members of his community. He said, “They are all members of my community. They went to Hurti village for a condolence visit and were returning to Tadai when suspected gunmen ambushed and killed them. “They were killed in broad daylight this afternoon. It is very sad and unfortunate.” Paul disclosed that one of the deceased was a newly graduated commander of Operation Rainbow, adding that the killing had thrown the community into mourning. He said, “The commander had just graduated. We are deeply saddened by this incident, especially given the security challenges our people have continued to face.” Also confirming the incident, an award-winning Nigerian conflict reporter from Bokkos, Masara Kim, said the two men were killed in the ambush while returning from the condolence visit. The deceased Operation Rainbow commander was said to have recently completed a refresher training programme for unit commanders in Jos, Kim added. Efforts to obtain further details from security authorities were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report. nigeria.title: Tinubu’s education reforms reach 3m tertiary students, Alausa tells opposition
nigeria.description: …Accuses opposition of misleading Nigerians, says government prioritising results over promises By Joseph Erunke, Abuja Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, has challenged opposition politicians, particularly former Labour Party presidential candidate, Peter Obi, to familiarise themselves with Nigeria’s education laws before criticising the Federal Government’s policies, insisting that nearly three million tertiary students are benefiting from President Bola Tinubu’s reforms. Alausa, who accused the opposition of deliberately misrepresenting the administration’s interventions, said criticisms of the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND, and other education policies were misplaced and failed to acknowledge the benefits Nigerians were already enjoying. The minister fired back at Obi on Monday during a briefing at the All Progressives Congress Presidential Campaign Council headquarters in Abuja, where he defended the Tinubu administration’s record in education ahead of the 2027 general elections. In a direct response to Obi’s criticisms, Alausa said the former presidential candidate needed to study the relevant legislation before making public statements about the government’s education financing arrangements. “What Mr Obi is saying is borne out of ignorance. He needs to read the law. This is the law of Nigeria,” the minister declared. He further accused Obi of misleading Nigerians, saying: “If Mr Obi wants to blame me and mislead the public and Nigerians, that tells you the kind of person he is.” At the centre of the disagreement is the four per cent development levy introduced under the Nigeria Tax Act, which Alausa said was designed to guarantee sustainable funding for the student loan scheme. He explained that 15 per cent of the proceeds from the levy was earmarked for NELFUND, insisting that the allocation was expressly provided for in the law and not an arbitrary government arrangement. nigeria.title: Two mass shootings claim 17 lives in South Africa
nigeria.description: By Juliet Umeh, Agency Report At least 17 people have been killed in two separate mass shootings in South Africa, with police yet to establish the motives behind the attacks, which occurred about 530 kilometres apart on Sunday. Eight people were found dead inside a bullet-riddled vehicle in Sweetwaters, outside Pietermaritzburg, while nine others were killed in a shack in Jeffsville, near the capital, Pretoria. Police spokesperson, Robert Netshiunda, said the identities of the eight victims in Sweetwaters were yet to be confirmed, although some families had approached authorities to assist. “It’s still too early to tell what the motive could have been and who could be behind the shooting because we are yet to identify the victims,” he said. In Jeffsville, six males and three females were found with gunshot wounds inside a four-room shack. Police spokesperson, Brenda Muridili, said officers were alerted at about 7:30 a.m. on Monday, although the shooting reportedly occurred between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. on Sunday. No arrests had been made as investigations continued. Gauteng Police Commissioner, Tommy Mthombeni, said the killings could be linked to a shooting in nearby Saulsville last year, which claimed 12 lives and left 13 others injured. He disclosed that one of Sunday’s victims was a person of interest in the previous attack, adding that police could not rule out retaliation. South Africa has recorded several deadly mass shootings in the past year. In September, 11 people, including a pregnant woman, were killed in an attack on a house near Durban, while another shooting at a tavern claimed 17 lives. Two separate shootings in Johannesburg in June also left 24 people dead, with police linking one to rival illegal mining gangs. Two other mass shootings in December last year claimed 21 lives. Police investigations into Sunday’s attacks are ongoing. The post Two mass shootings claim 17 lives in South Africa appeared first on Vanguard News .

nigeria.description: By Elizabeth Adegbesan Nigeria’s headline inflation rate declined to 14.06 per cent in October 2026 from 14.63 per cent recorded in September, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) has said. The NBS disclosed this in its latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released on Monday, also showing a decline in food inflation to 19.13 per cent in October from 19.59 per cent in the preceding month. According to the report, headline inflation stood at 18.97 per cent in October 2025, indicating a 4.91 percentage-point decline in the annual rate between October 2025 and October 2026. The statistics agency, however, reported an increase in the month-on-month headline inflation rate, which rose to 0.43 per cent in October from 0.06 per cent in September. It explained that the development indicated that the average price level increased at a faster rate in October than in the preceding month. “In October 2026, the Headline inflation rate stood at 14.06%, down from 14.63% in September 2026 and stood at 18.97% in the same month of the preceding year (October 2025),” the NBS stated. The report added that the October 2026 headline inflation rate represented a 4.91 percentage-point decline compared with the corresponding period of the previous year. “On a month-on-month basis, the Headline inflation rate in October 2026 was 0.43%, which was 0.38% higher than the rate recorded in September 2026 (0.06%). “This means that in October 2026, the rate of increase in the average price level was higher than the rate of increase in the average price level in September 2026,” the agency said. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine German Bundestag Lets Customs Freeze Crypto Over €100,000 Without a Criminal Case as the Bill Goes to the Bundesrat The German Bundestag on Thursday approved a government bill that would let customs freeze cryptocurrency and other assets worth more than €100,000 when their lawful origin appears implausible, without first opening a criminal case. Permanent confiscation would still take a finance-court judgment. The measure still needs the Bundesrat’s consent before a planned Jan. 1, 2027 start, and the timing of that upper-house vote remains unclear. The Bundestag passed the Customs Financial Justice Act, a Finance Ministry overhaul to strengthen the customs administration and fight financial crime, on Nov. 12. The federal government introduced the bill on Sept. 30. The Finance Committee recommended passage on Nov. 11, with the Christian Democrats, Social Democrats and Alternative for Germany in favor, The Left opposed and the Greens abstaining. Crypto is covered but not singled out Crypto is covered expressly, using the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets definition, but it is not singled out. The same administrative procedure applies to cash, cars, real estate and other property. It reaches only “significant” assets: generally those worth more than €100,000, or more than €50,000 if the asset must be entered in a public register, such as vehicles or land. Because crypto is not registered that way, the €100,000 threshold applies. Customs may estimate the value, and closely related items can be treated as one asset. Customs offices — not Germany’s Financial Intelligence Unit, which the same bill strengthens separately — may freeze those assets for up to 30 days without a criminal case if there are factual indications the origin is not lawful, meaning lawful acquisition “does not appear plausible.” A finance court may extend that hold once by 150 days. That extension is decided by a single judge, without a hearing, in an order that cannot be appealed. Filing a confiscation application stops the clock until the court rules, so the often-cited 180-day period is not a hard cap. Permanent confiscation still requires a finance-court panel to be convinced the origin is unlawful. The committee shifted that decision away from a single judge. entertainment.title: Tems Is Officially a 12-Time Grammy Nominee!
entertainment.description: Tems is officially a 12-time Grammy nominee after securing four nominations for the 69th Grammy Awards. Photo Credit: Tems/Instagram One, two, three… and now 12! Tems has added four more Grammy nominations to her record, bringing her career total to 12 ahead of the 69th Grammy Awards. The latest recognition also makes her the first Nigerian female artist to receive four nominations in a single Grammy year, with this year’s shortlist recognising her work across four categories. The Nigerian singer is in contention for Best Global Music Album with her 10-track EP, Love Is a Kingdom , and Best African Music Performance for “ Big Daddy ”. She has also earned nominations for Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song for “ What You Need ”. The four nominations give her one of the most extensive Nigerian representations at this year’s ceremony and bring her Grammy wins to two, following previous victories in 2023 and 2025. Her relationship with the Recording Academy began in 2022, when she received her first nomination for her contribution to Wizkid ‘s “ Essence ”, which was nominated for Best Global Music Performance at the 64th Grammy Awards. The following year brought three more nominations, this time for her work on Future’s “ Wait for U ” featuring Drake and Beyoncé ‘s Renaissance . She won her first Grammy that night, taking home Best Melodic Rap Performance for “Wait for U”, while also receiving nominations for Album of the Year and Best Rap Song. Tems earned another nomination at the 66th Grammy Awards in 2024 for “ Lift Me Up ”, her contribution to the Black Panther : Wakanda Forever soundtrack, in the Best Song Written for Visual Media category. She returned to the Grammys the following year with three nominations, including Best Global Music Album for her debut album, Born in the Wild , and Best R&B Song for “ Burning ”. Her second Grammy win came in the Best African Music Performance category, where “ Love Me JeJe ” took home the award at the 67th Grammy Awards in February 2025. Now, with four nominations for the 69th edition, Tems has added another significant chapter to her Grammy record. The ceremony will take place on Sunday, 7 February 2027, at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. entertainment.title: Wunmi Adelusi: Why Are We Still Hiding That We Use AI?
entertainment.description: Not long ago, I finished a piece of writing I was proud of — my thoughts, my argument, my structure. I had used an AI tool to help tighten the grammar and smooth the flow. And then, before sharing it, I went hunting through the text to delete every long dash. Why? Because the em dash has become the internet’s favourite “tell” that AI was involved. I was, quite literally, editing my work to hide a tool I had every right to use. When I caught myself doing it, I had to laugh. And then I had to ask: why the shame? It turns out I am not alone. Across a study spanning 47 countries, 57% of employees admit to concealing how they use AI at work. The reasons are almost entirely about reputation. In one recent survey of 5,000 desk workers, nearly half said they worried about appearing less capable or less competent, and a third feared they would simply look lazy. We are using the tools, and quietly scrubbing the fingerprints. There is even a quiet hypocrisy to it. Another survey says out of 7,200 adults, 46% said they would not disclose AI’s role in their own work while the remaining 54% said other people should. I had assumed this reticence was a particularly African trait. In my own experience, my colleagues in DC and Europe — my manager included — are refreshingly matter-of-fact about it. In one meeting recently, when asked to find a specific document in a shared folder, my manager cheerfully said he’d just let AI search it rather than disturb anyone’s work. Someone joked about his “secret agent,” and we all laughed. It was open, unbothered, upfront. I had concluded that we, of African descent, were simply more conservative, more inclined to glorify the heavy lifting, to wear “I stayed up all night doing it myself” as a badge of honour. But the research corrected me. This isn’t cultural; it’s universal. Employees across the US, UK, Europe, Latin America, Japan and Australia hide their AI use at strikingly similar rates. Even leadership does it. In some studies, managers conceal their AI use more than junior staff do. So perhaps the real question is why do we treat AI-assisted work as less credible than work done the hard way? I’ve even heard of recruiters downgrading CVs that look AI-generated, penalising the polish itself. But surely the more useful question is whether the substance behind it is real. A candidate who used a tool to sharpen how they present genuine experience hasn’t cheated; they’ve shown resourcefulness. The due diligence should be on verifying the claims, not on detecting the dashes. Screening out the tell, rather than testing the truth, risks rejecting capable people for the crime of being efficient. Because when you think about it, the logic is backwards. entertainment.title: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar Makes History as First Female Vice-Chancellor of UNIJOS
entertainment.description: Professor Patricia Mamko Lar, appointed as the 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor and first female Vice-Chancellor of the University of Jos. The University of Jos (UNIJOS) has officially appointed Professor Patricia Mamko Lar as its 11th substantive Vice-Chancellor, making her the first woman to occupy the position since the institution was established in 1971. Announced on Thursday, 12 November 2026 by the university’s Pro-Chancellor and Chairman of Council, Senator Grace Folashade Bent , during a special meeting of the 15th Governing Council, the historic appointment sees Professor Lar succeed Professor Tanko Ishaya as she takes the helm of the Plateau State institution. Born in Langtang, Plateau State, Professor Lar is a distinguished Professor of Medical Microbiology whose career has been deeply woven into the fabric of UNIJOS for nearly four decades. After earning her Bachelor of Science degree in Microbiology from Ahmadu Bello University, Zaria in 1986, she joined the University of Jos in 1987 as a Graduate Assistant in the Department of Medical Microbiology. She later went on to earn her Master’s degree in Medical Microbiology in 1989 and her PhD in Medical Parasitology in 1998 from the University of Lagos, followed by postdoctoral training at the Institute of Human Virology, University of Maryland in the United States under the NIH-Fogarty Fellowship Programme. Rising steadily through the academic ranks, she became an Associate Professor in 2012 before attaining full professorship in October 2015. Over the years, she has built an impressive body of work with more than 40 scholarly publications focusing on infectious diseases, including HIV/AIDS, malaria, antimicrobial resistance, and phytomedicine. Beyond the lecture hall and laboratory, Professor Lar has also served in key administrative roles at UNIJOS—including Head of the Department of Microbiology and Director of Linkages and Collaborations—and previously served a six-month tenure as Acting Vice-Chancellor of Yakubu Gowon University (formerly the University of Abuja) following her appointment by President Bola Tinubu in February 2025. Alongside her academic and leadership credentials, Professor Lar is a recognised advocate for women’s empowerment, having received the He4She Certificate of Award for Women Empowerment Activism in 2019. As she begins her five-year single term as UNIJOS’s first female substantive Vice-Chancellor after 55 years, she brings nearly four decades of institutional experience to the university’s top seat. technology.title: Hyperscale data centers use 2% of US electricity
technology.description: One flashpoint for the tech industry’s all-in push on Large Language Models has been the sudden rush to turn investment money into hyperscale data centers. The rush hasn’t allowed anyone to plan how to supply the required electricity cleanly or with minimal impact on ratepayers. Instead, it has been difficult to even collect information on what’s being built. A new study has tallied up energy use and estimated emissions for hyperscalers operating between May 2024 and April 2025 in the United States. They weren’t able to differentiate between AI compute and more traditional data services, but it provides a clear point of reference that could be tracked moving forward. Finding the centers The team started with a list of 675 facilities from a commercial database based on news reports, company statements, and satellite imagery. They dropped any that didn’t have a reported electrical capacity or that they couldn’t verify was a suitably large building with the expected cooling and electrical connection equipment. technology.title: Supreme Court keeps injunction against DEI grant defunding in place
technology.description: On Monday, the Supreme Court announced it would not hear an appeal of a lower court decision that blocked the government from canceling the grants of a handful of researchers whose funding had been revoked during the Trump administration's purge of DEI-related work. While the decision applies to only seven researchers in California, the lower court had ruled that the government's actions violated the First Amendment and so may have broad implications. The Supreme Court provided no discussion of its rejection, and no justices filed a dissent regarding the decision. The suit was initially filed by a large group of researchers at the University of California, contesting grants originally issued by a large number of federal agencies, from the National Institutes of Health to the Department of Transportation. At issue were grants that had been terminated because the agencies decided they violated a Trump executive order blocking the use of DEI. This occurred despite the fact that the government hadn't bothered to define DEI , and targeted grants were often identified by little more than a keyword search . Read full article Comments

technology.title: Attackers are using AI agents to automate cybercrime at 'industrial scale,' FBI and AWS warn
technology.description: Attackers are using open source AI penetration testing framework ARTEX to automate their attacks on banks, governments, energy and healthcare providers, and other critical sectors around the globe, according to security alerts from the FBI and Amazon Threat Intelligence. Between October 3 and November 5, Amazon’s MadPot honeypot threat sensors detected two ARTEX campaigns: one that allowed thieves to steal AI credentials at “industrial scale” to gain free access to models, and a second that generated deepfake videos to trick live selfie checks. In the first one, miscreants used AI agents to steal API keys, and then feed these keys into the ARTEX framework’s model gateway to power more agents searching for more AI model access keys. “Agents validated identities through each provider’s token and identity services, enumerated storage, assessed permission scope, and went after managed AI model services, secrets and parameter stores, and application identities,” AWS Chief Information Security Officer CJ Moses wrote in a blog post on Friday. Targets included LLM gateways and proxy platforms such as One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, and LiteLLM, and AI application builders Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, and Ollama. This campaign also used cloud credentials to gain stolen access to the models. In a second campaign, attackers used ARTEX to create real-time deepfake videos to trick identity verification (KYC) checks at two cryptocurrency exchanges, and forged ID photos to pass document checks. “The agents reverse-engineered one vendor’s liveness protocol in detail, documenting the face-detection event stream it sends, how it tracks face position during the check, and the coordinate system it uses to tell the user where to move,” Moses wrote. The agents did manage to complete the full movement sequence with the face positioned within 7 pixels of the target, but this feat was not enough, as the vendor’s server-side verdict rejected the deepfake in every attempt. In a separate session, agents built a real-time deepfake video pipeline on a single consumer-grade GPU using an open-source face animation model. This video achieved 11.5 frames per second, which Moses said is “close to what a live video check expects.” Meanwhile, agents also worked on the ID document checks, building synthetic camera metadata whose image dimensions matched the real values inside the JPEG file, and preserving the original camera compression tables that are usually replaced by re-saving an edited image. While the end goal was stealing cryptocurrency, the campaign illustrates how ARTEX runs several sessions simultaneously, with multiple agents working toward the same result. “One searched for ways to cash out, one worked on clearing account balances, one set up the deepfake video pipeline, and one carried out the verification bypass,” Moses wrote. technology.title: When will humans actually fly on Starship?
technology.description: The stunning return of Starship from the skies to a launch tower in South Texas answered some questions about the future of SpaceX's ambitious rocket program. Namely, it is now rapidly moving toward rapidly reusable launch. However, it raises other questions. For example, as Starship becomes fully reusable, when might humans fly on the vehicle? The short answer is pretty simple: If SpaceX prioritizes human spaceflight on Starship, it could happen reasonably quickly. The longer answer becomes more complicated and depends on what one means by human spaceflight. The first people to fly on Starship probably won't launch from Earth, or land here. Rather, they will probably be NASA's lunar astronauts. So there are different timelines for humans flying aboard Starship and landing on Earth. Read full article Comments

technology.title: HTML-in-Canvas ships and could make the web a lot more creative...and a lot stupider
technology.description: After two years of experimentation, the Chrome team shipped the HTML-in-Canvas API with Chrome 157. With it comes a new vision of how Web pages could be designed, for better or worse, allowing richer, more interactive elements but also more opportunities for annoying ads. “Previously, when creating visually demanding web apps, you had to choose between standard HTML elements and raw canvas contexts,” enthused one Google DevRel in a tutorial . “HTML-in-Canvas eliminates these trade-offs.” The Web API has been submitted for inclusion in the WHATWG HTML Living Standard , the ever-updating standard formerly known as HTML5 – for all the technologies that officially make up HTML (including Canvas itself). A Web API for the browser’s rendering engine Originally developed by Apple and standardized in 2014, the canvas tag is an HTML element that offers a space to render fluid graphics via JavaScript drawing commands. It creates a dedicated grid on screen, within which JavaScript can use a set of Canvas methods to draw lines, curves, text, gradients, and images. Or, the user’s GPU, via WebGL or WebGPU, can use the canvas to render 3D images and other custom effects. The downside of Canvas is that the regular HTML controls didn’t work inside the canvas itself. Formatting any text had to be done by hand. Interactivity was out, as were accessibility aids. Primarily developed by the Google Chromium team, HTML-in-Canvas allows JavaScript to place HTML commands within the canvas element, thanks to an attribute option within Canvas. If the canvas tag includes a content attribute of "drawable," the browser’s rendering engine prepares the HTML content inside the box so JavaScript can render it. While fully supported by Chrome and Chrome Android beginning with release 157, none of the other major browsers support the API yet (Microsoft Edge 157 – which is made of Chromium – unofficially appears to support at least some HTML-in-Canvas actions as well). The Web’s about to get lit Google posted a few possibilities of what can be done with HTML-in-Canvas. Developers can wrap HTML controls onto a 3D object. In one example , the user can turn the pages of a virtual book and even copy text out of the book itself. A video, complete with a set of controls , can be wrapped into an odd-sized canvas. The spec seems to work particularly well with JavaScript plug-ins, allowing coders to create entire 3D environments with Three.js , or to create charts with D3.js . Enthusiasts are already hacking against the spec with mad abandon. Developer Wes Bos put a notes app in the canvas , then used it as target practice by overlaying the app with some Duck Hunt-styled game code. HTML-in-Canvas “opens up the door to a lot of stupid use cases … but also a lot of really creative, interesting things where you can apply stylistic effects to HTML,” Bos explained on X . technology.title: China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion
technology.description: A new Top500 list of supercomputers has dropped, but little has changed. China remains uncontested with the most powerful supercomputer on the biannual ranking, and the US is not even close behind. The Middle Kingdom's LineShine super tops the list, boasting 2.2 exaFLOPS as measured by the High Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark. That's roughly 22 percent ahead of Uncle Sam’s biggest iron, Laurence Livermore National Laboratory’s El Capitan . But LineShine may not be the most efficient. Using 42.2 megawatts, LineShine’s lead comes at the expense of a noticeably higher power bill; not that that makes much of a difference. Number one is number one, and to add insult to injury, the National Supercomputing Centre in Shenzhen (NSCS) did it in spite of US export controls denying them access to American GPUs. The entire super is powered by 45,360 LingKun LX2 CPUs , each with 304 Arm v9.2 cores clocking to 1.5 GHz. The US is unlikely to reclaim the number one spot any time soon, though not for lack of trying. Under the Genesis Mission announced late last year, the Department of Energy is on track to deploy at least nine new supers. It just so happens that most of these will be smaller or AI-focused machines, with few truly large systems. Oak Ridge National Laboratory’s (ORNL) Lux supercomputer , built in collaboration with HPE and AMD, is one such example. Delivering 220 petaFLOPS of double-precision grunt in HPL, it’s certainly a potent system. Just two years ago it would have been a top 10 supercomputer, but it''l have to settle for number 14 on this fall’s Top500 ranking. Now, if you’re willing to turn the resolution slider down to FP4, peak performance jumps to somewhere north of 20 exaFLOPS. That’s fine for AI inference and even some training, but for running multi-physics sims on America's nuclear deterrent, the DoE has traditionally gone for something a bit bigger. ORNL’s upcoming Discovery system will certainly have enough grunt to give LineShine the boot. Details on the HPE Cray based system remain thin, but we do know it’ll be powered by a combination of AMD Venice CPUs and Instinct MI430X GPUs. Unlike most of the GPUs sold today, the MI430X hasn’t forsaken double-precision grunt for low-precision AI throughput. Each of these multi-die chips is estimated to deliver north of 200 teraFLOPS of FP64 matrix math. According to the DoE, Discovery will deliver somewhere between 3x to 5x the performance of Frontier, which would put its Rpeak somewhere between 5.1 and 8.5 exaFLOPS at FP64. As impressive as that might sound, China has proven that once you take power out of the equation, all it takes to claim the number one spot is scale. science.title: NASA Receives 16th Consecutive ‘Clean’ Financial Audit Opinion
science.description: Credit: NASA For the 16th consecutive year, NASA has received an unmodified, or “clean,” opinion from an external auditor on its fiscal year 2026 financial statements. The rating is the best possible audit opinion, certifying that NASA’s financial statements conform with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles for federal agencies and accurately present the agency’s financial position. “Our responsibility at NASA is to be disciplined stewards of the resources entrusted to us by the American people while delivering on the missions they expect from this agency,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “Our 16th consecutive clean audit reflects a long record of financial accountability, and we intend to pair that discipline with the urgency and execution required to take on the near-impossible missions ahead.” The 2026 Agency Financial Report provides key financial and performance information and demonstrates the agency’s commitment to transparency in the use of American taxpayers’ dollars. In addition, the 2026 report presents progress during the past year, and spotlights advancements in NASA missions, objectives, and workforce development with these financial resources. In fiscal year 2026 (FY 2026), NASA’s 10-day Artemis II mission successfully accomplished a test flight around the Moon with four crew members, delivering major human spaceflight milestones, such as the record‑breaking distance astronauts have traveled from Earth and global public engagement. NASA also announced a series of transformative agencywide initiatives designed to advance American leadership in space, including plans to build a Moon Base, which will be humanity’s first lunar outpost, and a place where astronauts will live, work, and explore near the Moon’s South Pole. NASA’s science advancements in FY 2026 included launching the agency’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, ahead of schedule, to study dark matter, dark energy, planets outside our solar system, as well as exploration of everything from nearby stars to distant galaxies. NASA’s experimental X-59 quiet supersonic aircraft achieved a major milestone when it flew faster than the speed of sound for the first time. The agency also: launched NASA Force with the U.S. Office of Personnel Management, a talent track designed to recruit and deploy the nation’s top engineers and technologists to support America’s space program; announced an agencywide realignment to increase mission focus; and welcomed additional Artemis Accords signatories committing to the safe, transparent, and responsible exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. science.title: Elon Musk says SpaceX’s Starship, already the largest rocket on Earth, will get even bigger with next-gen V4 model
science.description: null As usual, SpaceX and its founder Elon Musk are thinking big. The company recovered the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever on Saturday (Nov. 14), plucking it out of the sky with the "chopstick" arms of its Texas launch tower. It was a huge moment for SpaceX , bringing its vision of full and rapid rocket reuse much closer to reality. But Elon Musk isn't one to dwell on the past or rest on laurels, so he soon outlined an even more ambitious future for Starship. "Starship V4 will be ~70m [230 feet] long, which is roughly a 40% length increase and allows >60% more propellant load," Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Sunday evening (Nov. 15). "Engine count will be raised to 9, with 3 more Raptor-Vacuum engines added, and these will be higher-thrust V4 engines." The current version of Starship — the one that launched Friday (Nov. 13) on the vehicle's 15th test flight — is the V3. It's the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, standing 408 feet (124 m) tall when fully stacked with its Super Heavy first stage and Ship upper stage. V3's Ship is 171 feet (52 m) tall and features six of SpaceX's Raptor V3 engines. (The similarly reusable Super Heavy V3 booster is powered by 33 Raptors.) So, as Musk noted in his post, the V4 Ship will be quite an upgrade in size and power. This isn't the first we've heard about a V4 Starship. Back in August 2025, for example, Musk posted a graphic showing Starship's planned progression from the V2 to the V3 to the V4, which he said is expected to debut in 2027. science.title: What exactly is a light-day? Here's what Voyager 1's latest milestone means for the interstellar probe
science.description: null After nearly 50 years traveling through space, NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft is approaching a milestone no human-made object has reached before: a distance of one light-day from Earth. This milestone — which Voyager 1 is expected to reach on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (1016:07 GMT) — highlights the immense distances Voyager 1 has traveled and the challenges of communicating with spacecraft operating in the outer reaches of the solar system and beyond. Astronomers use a measurement known as a light-day to describe how far light travels in 24 hours. Light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (300,000 kilometers) per second, meaning one light-day is roughly 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers), according to a statement from NASA. Although the term light-day might sound like a measurement of time, it is actually a unit of distance, much like a light-year . Astronomers use light-based measurements because conventional miles and kilometers become increasingly difficult to comprehend when describing the enormous distances between objects in space. For perspective on how far Voyager 1 has travelled, sunlight takes about eight minutes and 20 seconds to reach Earth, meaning our planet is approximately 8.3 light-minutes from the sun. Radio signals traveling between Earth and Mars can take anywhere from three to 22 minutes, depending on the planets' positions in their orbits, according to the statement. By comparison, when Voyager 1 reaches one light-day from Earth , a radio signal sent from the probe will take a full 24 hours to reach mission controllers on Earth, and a command transmitted from Earth will take another 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. A NASA visualization showing Voyager 1 looking back towards the solar system as it approaches one light-day away from Earth. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) The communication delay affects how engineers operate spacecraft at such distances. Unlike spacecraft operating closer to Earth, which can receive commands and return data with relatively little delay, communicating with Voyager 1 requires mission controllers to account for the extended signal travel time when planning spacecraft operations, troubleshooting technical issues and evaluating the results of commands sent to the probe. Voyager 1 has been traveling away from Earth since its launch on Sept. 5, 1977 . Now cruising through interstellar space at nearly 38,000 mph (61,000 kph), the spacecraft has spent more than 49 years covering the distance that light can cross in a single day. Even at that speed, Voyager 1 is moving relatively slowly compared with light itself. Its twin, Voyager 2 , which launched in 1977 on a different trajectory, is expected to reach the same one-light-day milestone in November 2035. As Voyager 1 and, eventually, Voyager 2 continue their journeys through interstellar space , their growing distances from Earth offer a measure of both the reach of human exploration and the communication challenges

Speaking alongside former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival in Tenerife, Canary Islands, on Oct. 18, Glover opened up about the challenges of preparing his family for his riskiest mission yet. "This is maybe the greatest challenge of my astronaut career," Glover said. Glover joined NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1 , 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being New Scientist , I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct. I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of Terminator alongside the utopia of Star Trek . I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to population projections , which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece. science.title: The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18! Here's what you need to know
science.description: null The Leonid meteor shower peaks Nov. 17-18 sending shooting stars and fireballs across the autumn sky as Earth passes through a stream of debris left by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle. Up to 15 meteors could be spotted per hour under perfect dark sky conditions on the night of Nov. 17-18, according to the International Meteor Organisation . NASA, meanwhile, has given a more conservative rate of less than three meteors per hour — time will tell. Leonid meteors appear to race away from a point of origin, or radiant, in the constellation Leo, which glistens high above the southeastern horizon in the hours before dawn in mid-November. Both Jupiter and Mars will be separated by just a few degrees in the constellation Leo on the night of the peak, making it particularly easy to find in 2026! When is the best time to look for Leonid meteors? The best time to spot Leonids is in the hours before dawn on Nov. 18, when the radiant will reach its highest point in the southeastern sky, maximizing the amount of meteors that may be seen skimming through Earth's atmosphere . By then, the waxing moon will have set, leaving darker skies and a better chance of spotting fainter meteors. Shooting stars that appear close to the radiant will strike Earth almost head-on, leaving the shortest trails. Instead, find a patch of sky a short distance away from the constellation Leo, where the meteors will be at their most impressive, and give your eyes 20-30 minutes to fully adapt to the dark. Why are the Leonids special? As if shooting stars weren't enough, the Leonid shower is also known for spawning dazzling fireballs and long-lasting Earth-grazing meteors , which strike our atmosphere at an oblique angle, leaving long trains as they skim through before passing back out into space. The shower is also capable of producing magnificent meteor storms when Earth passes through particularly dense trails of debris left behind by Comet 55P/Tempel-Tuttle, which orbits the sun approximately every 33 years. Sadly, we'll have to wait a bit for the next big show. According to the Planetary Society , another Leonid meteor storm could occur as early as 2031, while a study released in August 2026 predicts potentially spectacular displays in 2033 and 2034. science.description: Construction work on an AI data centre in Texas covering nearly 40 square kilometres, which will have a capacity of 600 megawatts Backyard Productions/Alamy The largest data centres in the US are using roughly the same amount of power collectively each year as one of the country’s major states, according to new figures that underscore the size and impact these massive facilities are having on local power grids. The rapid development of artificial intelligence systems has triggered a “fast and furious” expansion of data centres across the US, in particular of very large “hyperscale” data centres that support AI tools, cloud computing and large language models, says Francesca Dominici at Harvard University. But tracking the power consumption and carbon emissions impact of these facilities is difficult, as many data centre operators don’t publicly report such information. Advertisement Read more SpaceXAI data centre may have led to Mississippi air pollution spike Together with colleagues, Dominici spent two years pulling together information on 403 hyperscale data centres in the US to estimate their electricity consumption and associated carbon dioxide emissions. “Doing these measurements took an enormous amount of work,” she says. The team estimates that the hyperscale data centres collectively used about 82 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity between May 2024 and April 2025, equivalent to about 1.8 per cent of total US electricity use. This electricity use outstrips the annual power consumption of states such as Missouri, Kentucky and New Jersey. The upper bound of the team’s estimate – 99 TWh per year – would see hyperscale data centres rival the annual power consumption of states such as Indiana, Michigan and Washington. This vast power consumption has a significant climate impact. The researchers estimate that roughly 54 per cent of attributed generation was supplied by fossil fuel sources, with annual carbon dioxide emissions reaching 25.7 million tonnes – equivalent to the emissions from 67 natural gas power plants . science.title: Could there be an ancient alien satellite in Earth's orbit? How the 'Black Knight' conspiracy theory has survived for over 100 years
science.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

In the final days of 1998, as astronauts aboard NASA's Space Shuttle Endeavor were working during one of the early missions to assemble the International Space Station , crew members from the STS-88 mission captured photographs of a dark colored, unusually shaped object drifting through space. Despite its unusual appearance in the photographs, the object had a conventional explanation, and one that was known to the astronauts at that time: it was one of several thermal covers that had been wrapped around trunnion pins used in the space station's construction. Upon noticing the "escape" of one of the covers, Mission Commander Bob Cabana remarked over the radio to fellow astronaut Jerry Ross that "one of the thermal covers got away from you." Seeing the cover drifting away, a frustrated Ross snapped a photograph of it. Yet despite the innocuous story behind the images, they have nonetheless helped fuel belief in an unusual Space Age conspiracy theory: one involving the alleged presence of an ancient satellite, presumably of alien origin, that has long been orbiting our planet — perhaps since the end of the last Ice Age. According to proponents of this theory, the object photographed by Ross in 1998 is actually what many call the " Black Knight Satellite ," and is only one piece of evidence they point to in a long succession of unrelated — and often misinterpreted — events in modern history that supposedly lend further evidence to the alleged alien spacecraft's existence. So how did such a legend gain traction in the first place, with some versions alleging that NASA and the U.S. government have worked to conceal evidence of the alleged space object's existence from the public? Odd detections at Colorado Springs Depending on which version of the story you come across, the strange roots of the Black Knight conspiracy theory might be traced all the way back to the nineteenth century, when the famous inventor Nikola Tesla began detecting unusual electrical signal s while conducting radio experiments at his laboratory in Colorado Springs. At the time, Tesla considered whether the signals might be communications from intelligent aliens on nearby planets, although the likely source had actually been terrestrial radio interference. Notably, Tesla also never claimed that the emissions might be coming from an object in Earth's orbit; nonetheless, some proponents of the Black Knight Satellite theories have incorporated Tesla's experiments into the mythos, suggesting they may represent some of the earliest detections of a mysterious object lurking near Earth. science.description: null The comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid) discovered by the Euclid mission. (Image credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, M. Pöntinen et al. 2026) The Euclid space telescope has discovered its first comet, called comet C/2026 S1, or comet Euclid for short. What is it? (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) The Euclid mission, a European Space Agency mission that launched in 2023 with contributions from NASA, spotted this previously undetected comet approximately 807 million miles (1.3 billion kilometers) away in observations captured between Sept. 16 and 24. "I was excited to see my software flag a 'streak' smeared across several images – the result of a fast-moving object. By predicting its position I could identify it in other images, in total finding it in five image sets. Further inspection revealed that it had a fuzzy cloud around it, indicative of an active object like a comet that is shedding dust and gas," Mikko Pöntinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki who made the initial discovery with a Solar System Objects Science Working Group within the Euclid Consortium, said in a statement . Following these observations, the team diligently checked current records of comets to ensure that this was, in fact, something new to us. An close up view of comet C/2026 S1 (Euclid). (Image credit: ESA/Euclid) Why is it incredible? Euclid is a mission designed to capture long, slow observations of deep space and distant galaxies and collect data to help scientists better unravel the mysteries of dark energy and dark matter. It was in not explicitly designed in any way to capture imagery of fast-moving comet hurtling through our solar system. But still, the space telescoped managed to catch this comet whirling between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. This finding shows that Euclid can be used for more than it was intended, and that in the future scientists could use it to intentionally target other comets in the far reaches of our solar neighborhood. These kinds of observations can also help researchers to identify "noise" like comet trails in Euclid's field of view.

science.title: Dream Chaser space plane gets landing approval for debut mission in 2027
science.description: null The Dream Chaser space plane just cleared a major hurdle ahead of its planned spring 2027 spaceflight debut. Dream Chaser just received U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) approval for its return to Earth on that robotic mission, either at the space shuttle landing facility at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida or at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. "Thank you to the FAA for its collaboration and support of commercial space innovation," representatives of Sierra Space, the Colorado company that builds Dream Chaser, wrote on X on Monday (Nov. 9). The FAA's environmental assessment found that Dream Chaser "would not significantly impact the quality of the human environment" under the National Environmental Policy Act, the agency stated . (It should also be noted that the U.S. has lately been suggesting that environmental laws should be bypassed to meet quickly rising demand for launches and landings.) For example, for a potential return at Vandenberg, "sonic booms are anticipated but would be temporary, short in duration, and limited to 1.1 PSF [pounds per square foot] or less, which is similar to a thunderclap," the FAA stated. The 30-foot-long (9 meters) Dream Chaser has been in development for more than two decades. It has yet to launch to space, though it has completed a couple of drop tests from the air. Dream Chaser was an entrant in NASA's Commercial Crew series of contracts to ferry astronauts to and from the International Space Station (ISS), but it didn't end up making the cut; in 2014, NASA picked Boeing's Starliner and SpaceX's Crew Dragon to provide this taxi service. The following year, Sierra Nevada Corporation — then the entity in charge of Dream Chaser — unveiled a cargo version of the space plane. In 2016, NASA selected the company to conduct at least six uncrewed cargo flights to the ISS, but development delays repeatedly pushed those missions into the future. Dream Chaser was originally expected to fly those robotic resupply missions on United Launch Alliance's workhorse Atlas V rocket. A few years ago, however, the space plane switched over to Vulcan Centaur , the successor to the venerable Atlas V. Dream Chaser was supposed to ride on Vulcan's second-ever mission but wasn't ready in time, so that flight went ahead in October 2024 without the space plane. Sierra Space is now targeting spring 2027 for Dream Chaser's first liftoff, which will be a free-flying test mission in Earth orbit. The company is now pursuing many types of contracts for Dream Chaser, anticipating a mix of missions for NASA, the U.S. military and private companies — including the consortiums that plan to build commercial space stations. Indeed, Sierra Space is a member of one such consortium — the group that plans to build an outpost known as Orbital Reef .

science.title: A Magna Carta for the stars: King Charles III takes on space sustainability
science.description: null We live in the era of the satellite. They power our phones, banking infrastructure, navigational systems and internet, while providing stunning imagery and data that can be used to direct emergency services, feed weather forecasts and help coordinate military assets. But low-Earth orbit is not an infinite resource. It's starting to get crowded, with over 16,000 satellites and over 1.2 million pieces of debris currently circling our planet at incredible speeds. And if not managed properly, the results could be catastrophic. "In the early days of the space age actors could more or less ignore the other actors," Peter Martinez, executive director of the Secure World Foundation told Space.com. "You know the big sky paradigm, right? You can do what you want because the chances of your actions affecting others are minuscule." As noted by Martinez, the modern orbital landscape is radically different from those early frontier days, especially since the mid 2010s and the advent of satellite megaconstellations. "Nowadays, we really do have to worry about orbital congestion, and because space is out of sight for most people, we don't." Each new rocket launch leaves a footprint on the orbital environment, whether it be the satellite payloads they place in orbit or the pieces of inert hardware they leave behind such as an interstage adapter or rocket body. All of those objects create an ever-increasing risk of collisions. 130 million pieces of debris are currently estimated to be orbiting Earth. (Image credit: ESA) In a worst case scenario, clouds of debris spawned by colliding spacecraft could create a cascading effect known as the Kessler syndrome , with the potential to render the orbital environment completely unusable, trapping us on Earth . Enter King Charles III's Astra Carta, an all-encompassing roadmap to space exploration that launched on June 28, 2023 with a clear but ambitious mandate — to place sustainability at the core of humanity's presence beyond Earth. What is the Astra Carta? The Astra Carta stands as the space-focused sibling of the Terra Carta — a voluntary framework that launched in 2021 with the goal of safeguarding Earth's natural splendor by championing a transition to global sustainability practices and environmental responsibility. Both names were chosen to draw comparison with the Magna Carta, a royal charter that served as an early foundation for the English Legal system and modern day democracies . The principles enshrined in the Astra Carta have the potential to be similarly transformative if taken to heart. "I have long felt that protecting space that immediately surrounds our planet is one of those issues few recognize as important, but like so many of our present challenges, that were ignored for too long, if we do not address it quickly, it will come back to haunt us in a big way," the then-Prince of Wales stated in a message to participants of the 4th Summit for Space Sustainability in June 2022. science.description: null Voyager 1 is celebrating a big milestone as it approaches its 50th birthday: reaching one light-day away from Earth. NASA's long-running interstellar Voyager 1 probe will mark one light-day of distance from Earth on Nov. 18, when the spacecraft is 49 years, two months and 11 days old. The agency recently stated the record distance, which will be reached at 5:16:07 a.m. EST (101607 GMT) is "a huge milestone by any measure, and a day worth celebrating." During the light-day crossover, Voyager will be in contact with the Madrid station of the three-antenna Deep Space Network that monitors all deep-space missions. The spacecraft is currently making its way through the constellation Ophiuchus from the perspective of Earth, said Jeffrey Hayes, a NASA official whose work includes Voyager 1. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) "This [milestone] essentially kicks off the year's worth of celebrations leading up to the 50th anniversary in August and September of next year," added Hayes, who is discipline scientist in the agency's astrophysics and heliophysics divisions, in a livestreamed discussion with NASA's Night Sky Network on Nov. 4. Going the distance Voyager 1 is the farthest spacecraft from Earth, after launching from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977 a few weeks after its twin, Voyager 2 . NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft launches atop a Titan/Centaur-6 rocket from Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Sept. 5, 1977. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/KSC) A light-day, as the name implies, represents the distance that light travels in a single day. In other words, at one light-day, a radio-wave message to Voyager 1 takes 24 hours to get to the spacecraft — which is roughly 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers) from Earth. Voyager's response then takes another day to get back to our planet. Voyager 2 — which is at a distance of 13.5 billion miles (21.7 billion km) from our planet — won't hit the light-day milestone until 2035, NASA stated. While the agency has not offered recent estimates for how long the two spacecraft will last, in 2022 Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, said they may keep operating into the 2030s . The two spacecraft had initial funding to survey Jupiter and Saturn, although NASA did launch them at a time when the planets aligned in such a way to bring Voyager 2 past Uranus and Neptune if funding continued — which it did. Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 7129: Star Formation with Jets from Webb Explanation: How do stars form? To help answer this question, NASA used the James Webb Space Telescope to take the featured detailed image of the star-forming region NGC 7129 in infrared light . Star formation progresses when gravity pulls together massive amounts of gas, but soon things can get complicated when previously formed stars emit powerful jets and winds — and some then explode . Opaque dust can form in the cool atmospheres of stars and, when dispersed, can obstruct visible-light images. Many stars can be seen to be forming in the featured image , with the young stars on the left, in the gold-colored gas, typically being more mature than the young stars on the right — in the red region. Jets and wind s likely cause the filamentary nature of the red-colored gas. Studying stars at different stages of development bolsters understanding about what physical processes are most important and when.
